transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, what brings me in is... it's this thing that keeps happening down at the museum. I spend a lot of time there these days, just helping out since I'm not working anymore. They've actually got this incredible new watercolor exhibit up right now—mostly coastal scenes, lots of blues and greys. Reminds me of when my brother used to live out in Oregon. We’d drive up Highway 101 and just watch the fog roll in off the water... it's a beautiful drive, if you ever get the chance you really should take it. They have these little crab shacks right on the water that are just fantastic. 

But, uh, anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the museum. So, the folks there will be talking right to me, you know, maybe going over the plans for the next art walk, and I’ll be looking right at them. But then I suddenly realize I completely missed the middle part of what they just said. I have to stop them and ask them to run it by me again. It's just getting a bit embarrassing to keep doing that.
Do you think you actually heard them talking but your mind wandered, or do you feel like you just didn't hear what they said at all?

I definitely hear them talking. It's not my hearing, I had that checked a couple years ago. The guy at the clinic said my hearing was actually pretty good for a guy my age. He had this whole setup with the soundproof booth and the little button you press... reminded me of being back in grade school when the nurse would come around with those big clunky headphones. 

But yeah, I hear the words, it's just... my mind is somewhere else. Like the other day, Shirley was telling me about the new display cases, and I was looking right at her, but in my head I was thinking about whether I left the sprinkler on in the backyard. The tomatoes are really coming in nice this year, by the way. I've got these Big Boys that are just huge. I had to put up extra stakes just to keep the vines from snapping. But yeah, I hear them, I just... I don't know where my brain goes.
Do you think you're more likely to zone out like that when you're feeling stressed or anxious about something?

Stress? No, I wouldn't really say it's stress. I mean, I don't have a whole lot to be stressed about these days, what with being retired and all. It's actually been real nice just taking it easy. My buddy Frank—he retired about five years before me—he always told me, "Just wait till you don't have to set an alarm clock anymore." And he was right, it's the best feeling in the world. Frank used to work down at the old auto plant before it closed up. Good guy, makes a mean brisket. He's got one of those big offset smokers in his backyard... takes him like fourteen hours to do a brisket right, but man, is it worth it. We usually go over there for the Fourth of July. 

But anyway, no, it's not really when I'm anxious. It just sort of happens whenever. I could be perfectly relaxed, just sitting there listening, and poof, my brain just takes a little vacation.
Do you find that you zone out more often when you're listening to something that doesn't particularly interest you?

Well, I guess... maybe? But honestly, I can zone out even when it's something I'm really interested in. Like the other week, we had this guest speaker come into the museum to talk about the history of the local railroads. I love trains. Ever since I was a kid, my dad used to take me down to the railyard on Sunday afternoons just to watch the freights roll through. He worked for the B&O Railroad for thirty-five years, mostly in the switchyard. He had this old pocket watch he used to carry, kept perfect time... I actually still have it sitting on my dresser. Needs a good cleaning, though. The glass is getting a little cloudy. I should probably take it down to that watch repair place on Main Street, if it's still open. You know, a lot of those old mom-and-pop shops have been closing down lately. It's a real shame, you just don't get the same kind of service at the big chain stores. 

But, uh, what was I... oh, the train lecture. Right. So, I was really looking forward to it, sitting right in the second row, but about ten minutes in, I caught myself staring at the pattern on the ceiling tiles and realized I hadn't heard a word the guy said for I don't know how long. So, yeah, it doesn't really seem to matter if I'm interested or not.
Are you finding that this zoning out is causing problems for you in your daily activities?

Well, it's starting to, I guess. At the museum, anyway. I've been volunteering there for, oh, going on seven years now. Started right after I retired. It's a nice little local history and art museum, nothing too fancy, but we get a good crowd on the weekends. We do these guided art walks through the galleries, and I used to love leading them. I'd read up on all the local artists... did you know we have a painter from around here who actually had a piece in the Smithsonian for a while? Eleanor something... I can't remember her last name right now, but she painted these beautiful watercolors of the river valley. The river used to be a lot higher back then, before they put the dam in up north. Used to flood out the lower fields every spring. My uncle had a farm down that way, grew mostly corn and soybeans. He lost a whole crop one year to the flooding, just completely washed out. It was a real mess, took them weeks to clean up all the mud and debris that got left behind. 

But anyway, with the art walks... I just don't feel confident doing them anymore. I'll be right in the middle of explaining a piece, and I'll zone out, and then I lose my place and I'm just standing there looking at a group of people. And the other folks at the museum, Shirley and the rest of the board, I think they've noticed. They've been quietly shifting some of the planning pieces and the organizing stuff away from me. They're real nice about it, say they just want to "lighten my load," but I know it's because I keep missing things when we're having our meetings.
Do you feel upset or frustrated when you realize you've zoned out and missed something?

Well, upset? I don't know if upset is the right word. Maybe a little embarrassed, you know? Like when I'm standing there with Shirley and I realize she's been talking for five minutes and I have no idea what she said. Shirley's a saint, really. She's been running the museum board since... oh, gosh, it has to be the late nineties. She used to be a home ec teacher at the high school. Taught both my girls how to sew, actually. My youngest, Sarah, she got so good at it she made her own prom dress. It was this beautiful blue satin thing, looked like something you'd buy at a fancy department store in the city. Cost a fortune in fabric, though. My wife and I drove all the way out to that big fabric warehouse off Route 9 just to find the right shade of blue. Took us all afternoon, and then we stopped at this little diner on the way back. Best cherry pie I've ever had. I wonder if that diner is still there... they had these red vinyl booths that squeaked every time you moved. 

But, uh, no, I wouldn't say I get really upset about zoning out. It's just more of a... a nuisance, I guess. I just kind of shake my head and try to catch up.
Are your relationships with family or friends being affected by your zoning out?

Well, no, I don't think so. My wife hasn't said anything about it, anyway. She's usually pretty busy herself these days, out in the garden from sunup to sundown. She's got this whole system for her heirloom tomatoes. You know, you can't just plant them and leave them be; you have to pinch the suckers off the vines or they get all wild and don't produce as much fruit. We had so many tomatoes last August we didn't know what to do with them. We were giving them away in plastic grocery bags to all the neighbors. 

Old Mr. Henderson next door, he took a whole bushel and made his own pasta sauce. He's Italian, moved here from Brooklyn back in the eighties, I think. Used to run a bakery downtown before he retired. Man, he made the best cannolis. I haven't had a really good cannoli in years. The bakeries around here now, they just use that pre-made filling out of a plastic bucket, and it's always way too sweet, you know? It just doesn't taste authentic. You need real ricotta. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, my friends and family. Right. Yeah, no, I don't think anyone's upset with me or anything like that. We all get along just fine.
Do you think you could recall what was being discussed if someone reminded you about it right after you zoned out?

Well, I suppose it depends on how quick they catch me. If Shirley says, "Hey, did you hear what I said about the new display cases?" I might be able to pull it back. The new display cases, by the way, they're supposed to be coming in from a supplier in Ohio. We had a devil of a time finding ones that were the right height for the antique dolls. The old ones we had were donated by the historical society back in '85, and the glass was getting all wavy. You know how old glass does that? It settles at the bottom over time, makes everything look kind of distorted. My grandmother had a mirror in her hallway like that. You'd look in it and your face would look like it was melting off. Scared my daughters half to death when they were little. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, if I could remember if they reminded me. Yeah, probably not. Even if they jogged my memory, I'd probably just realize I hadn't been listening at all. I usually just have to ask them to repeat the whole thing.
Do you think you would be able to recall the conversation if you tried to focus really hard on remembering it after you zoned out?

Well, I don't really know if that would work. I mean, if I wasn't listening in the first place, there's nothing really up here to focus on, you know? It's kind of like trying to find a tool in the garage when you know you didn't put it back in the toolbox. 

Speaking of the garage, I was out there yesterday looking for my good socket wrench. The Craftsman one, from back in the seventies. They just don't make them like that anymore. Now you buy a set at the hardware store and it's all that cheap metal. You try to tighten a bolt on the lawnmower and the socket just strips right out. My lawnmower has been giving me a heck of a time lately, actually. It's a riding mower, but the carburetor keeps getting gunked up. I think it's the ethanol in the gas these days, it just eats right through the plastic fuel lines. Old Mr. Henderson, the neighbor I was telling you about, he swears by this fuel stabilizer stuff that comes in a little red bottle. He buys it by the case down at the auto parts store on Main Street. The guy who runs that store used to play football with my brother, actually. Small world, isn't it?

But, um... wait, focusing? Right, the conversation. Yeah, no, focusing really hard doesn't do much good for me. If the words didn't go in, they just aren't there, no matter how hard I squint and try to dig around for them.
Do you think you would be able to recall the start of a conversation if someone reminded you about it later, even if you zoned out in the middle?

Well, I suppose if they reminded me about how it started... maybe? I mean, sometimes I can remember the very beginning before I drift off. Like the other day, my daughter called. She lives over in Springfield now, bought this little split-level house a couple years ago. The market was crazy then, people putting in offers twenty thousand over asking without even seeing the place. She got lucky, though, the previous owners were an older couple moving into an assisted living place, and they just wanted a quick sale. Left all their window treatments, too, which was nice, because custom blinds cost a small fortune nowadays. 

Anyway, she called, and I remember she started off talking about her dog, Buster. He's a golden retriever mix, sweetest thing, but he's got this terrible habit of digging under the fence. He got out last week and ended up three streets over at the elementary school right when the kids were at recess. Total chaos, apparently. The principal had to come out with a hot dog from the cafeteria to lure him into the office. 

But, uh... where was I going with that? Oh, right, the beginning of the conversation. I remembered she started with Buster, but honestly, by the time she was halfway through the story, I was looking out the window at the neighbor's gutters and completely lost the thread. So, even if someone reminds me how it started, I still don't know what happened in the middle. The middle is just a blank spot.
Do you think you could recall what was being discussed if someone reminded you about it right after you zoned out and you tried to pay close attention to the reminder?

Well, if they reminded me right away and I really tried to listen to the reminder... I don't know, it's still tough. Actually, that's kind of what brings me in here in the first place. Like, people down at the museum will be talking right to me about the next art walk we're hosting. We do them every first Friday of the month, usually. The local artists set up little booths, and we keep the museum open late. Last month we had this fellow who does these amazing sculptures out of scrap metal. Welds old car parts and silverware together. He made this owl out of spoons that was just incredible. Wanted three hundred dollars for it, though, which seemed a bit steep, but I suppose art is subjective, isn't it? My wife used to paint watercolors, mostly landscapes. She had an eye for color, always getting the sunset just right over the lake... 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the art walk. So, they'll be talking right to me about it, and I'll be looking right at them, nodding along, and then I just... realize I completely missed the middle of what they said. Even if they try to remind me, the middle part is just gone. I usually just have to swallow my pride and ask them to run the whole thing by me again.
Are you finding that this zoning out is causing problems for you outside of your activities at the museum?

Well, it's... yeah, it's definitely spilling over. I mean, the museum is a big part of my week. I've been volunteering there since I retired from the post office. Thirty years sorting mail, you wouldn't believe the things people try to send through the post. Once, I swear, a fellow tried to mail a whole, unpackaged coconut. Just slapped a label and some stamps right on the shell. The sorting machine didn't know what to do with it, jammed the whole line up for two hours. My supervisor, Gary, he was furious. Gary was always a bit high-strung, though. He had this little vein on his forehead that would pulse when he got mad. He ended up retiring early and moving to Florida, bought a condo down in Boca, I think. Or maybe it was Naples. One of those places with the golf courses everywhere. I tried golf once, but I just don't have the patience for it. You hit the ball, you walk after it, you hit it again... seems like a good way to ruin a nice walk, if you ask me. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the zoning out. Yeah, it's... it's causing some real trouble at the museum. The folks in the group, they're nice about it, but they've had to quietly shift some of the planning pieces away from me. Like, I used to handle the vendor coordination for the art walks, but now Susan is doing most of it. And honestly, I've just stopped feeling confident leading the walks the way I used to. I'm always worried I'm going to lose my train of thought right in front of a crowd of people. It's frustrating, you know? You get to be my age, you want to feel useful, not like a liability.
Do you think you would be able to recall the conversation if you wrote it down right after it happened?

Write it down right after? Well, I suppose I could try that, if I had a pen handy. I used to carry one of those nice Parker pens, the kind with the gold arrow clip. My father gave me one when I graduated high school. Back then, a good pen really meant something, you know? People actually wrote letters. My aunt Mildred used to write me these long, sprawling letters from Seattle. She lived out there near the Pike Place Market. Used to send us smoked salmon every Christmas in the mail. Best salmon I ever had, really ruined store-bought fish for me. You just can't get that same genuine alder-wood smoke flavor out of a vacuum-sealed plastic pouch... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, writing the conversation down. Right. Well, the problem is, like I was saying before about why I even came in here... if the folks at the museum are standing there talking right to me about the next art walk, and I'm looking right at them, and then I realize I've completely missed the middle of what they were saying... well, writing it down afterward doesn't really fix it, does it? Because that middle part is already gone. I can't write down what my brain didn't catch. I'd still just have to stop them and ask them to run the whole thing by me again just so I'd have something to put on the paper.
Do you think you could recall what was being discussed if you were able to go back and hear the conversation again from the beginning?

Hear it again from the beginning? Well, I suppose if someone had a tape recorder going, that might work. They used to make those little dictaphones, you know, with the tiny cassette tapes. My buddy Carl, he was a claims adjuster for the insurance company, used to carry one of those everywhere. He'd walk around a wrecked car, just talking into this little black box, detailing every dent and scratch. Fascinating job, really, seeing all those smashed up cars. He told me once about a fellow who drove a brand new Cadillac right into a swimming pool. Thought he was in reverse, hit the gas, and splash. Can you imagine? The upholstery was completely ruined, smelling like chlorine and swamp water. Carl said the guy was more worried about his golf clubs in the trunk than the actual car. Golfers, I tell you, they have their priorities all mixed up...

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, hearing it from the beginning. Right. Well, like I was saying before, the issue is that when I'm standing there, and they're talking right to me about the art walk or whatever, I'm looking right at them. But then I just... I miss the middle part. It's just a blank. So, sure, if I could magically rewind time and hear the whole thing again from the start, I might catch it the second time around. But in real life, I can't do that. I just have to stop them and ask them to run the whole thing by me again. It's the only way I can get what I missed.
Do you think you would be able to recall the conversation if you were fully focused and paying attention from the beginning?

Fully focused from the beginning? Well, I certainly try to be. I even started drinking more coffee before I go in, just to make sure I'm sharp. We used to just brew a pot of Folgers, you know, the big plastic red tub? Kept one in the breakroom at the post office for thirty years. But my daughter, she bought me one of those fancy machines for my birthday. The ones that take the little plastic pods. Keurig, I think it's called. It's convenient, sure, but the pods cost an arm and a leg if you buy them at the grocery store. And the coffee comes out so hot you'll burn your tongue if you aren't careful. I burned my tongue on a bowl of clam chowder once up in Boston, couldn't taste a thing for three days. Miserable trip, really, it rained the entire weekend... 

Anyway, sorry, I'm wandering again. Being fully focused. The thing is, doctor, like I keep saying, I *think* I am focused. That's exactly what brings me in here. I'll be standing there at the museum, looking right into someone's eyes, paying attention right from the start when they start talking about the next art walk. I'm locked in. But then, out of nowhere, I just realize I've completely missed the middle of whatever they just said. It doesn't seem to matter that I was trying to focus at the beginning. My brain just drifts off anyway, and I still have to swallow my pride and ask them to run it by me again.
Do you think you would be able to recall the conversation if someone reminded you about it right after you zoned out and you were able to see the person's lips moving and hear their voice clearly?

See their lips moving and hear them clearly? Well, my hearing is perfectly fine, you know. I actually just had it checked a few months ago by Dr. Henderson over on Elm Street. Nice fellow, collects antique clocks. His whole waiting room just ticks. Tick, tick, tick. Dozens of them on the walls. Drives some people absolutely crazy, but I always found it rather soothing. Reminds me of my grandfather's house up in Vermont. He had this massive grandfather clock in the hallway that chimed every quarter hour. You'd think a racket like that would keep you up at night, but you really do get used to it. Actually, the silence is what wakes you up if somebody forgets to wind it and it stops... 

But what was the question? Oh, seeing their lips and hearing them. Right. Well, Doc, I feel like a bit of a broken record today, but that's exactly the thing I've been trying to explain about my shifts at the museum. I *am* looking right at them. I can see their lips moving just fine, and I hear their voices perfectly clearly. The volume isn't the issue at all. I'll be standing there, staring right at their face while they go on about the art walk schedules, and then I just... realize I missed a whole chunk of it. The middle part is just gone. 

Even if they snap me out of it right then and remind me we were talking, it doesn't help me remember what they actually said, because my brain never recorded it in the first place. I still just have to apologize and ask them to run the whole thing by me again.
Do you think you zone out more often when you're listening to someone you're not very interested in?

Someone I'm not interested in? Well, I suppose that happens to everybody, doesn't it? My neighbor Bill, for instance, he can talk for forty-five minutes about the proper way to clean aluminum siding. He bought this heavy-duty power washer last summer, gas-powered, loud as a jet engine. Sprayed my rose bushes by accident and nearly took the petals clean off. My wife loved those roses. We planted them the year we moved in, back in '87. Soil was so rocky I broke two shovels just digging the holes. Bought them at the old hardware store downtown before it turned into that fancy pet bakery. Have you seen that? Ten dollars for a dog biscuit shaped like a bone, just ridiculous... 

Anyway, sorry, my mind is wandering again. You were asking if I only zone out when I'm bored. The truth is, Doc—and I know I keep saying this exact same thing—but it's what brought me in here in the first place. It happens even when I *want* to hear it. Like I said, people at the museum will be talking right to me about the next art walk, which I genuinely enjoy helping with, and I'll be looking right at them, and then I just realize I missed the middle of what they said. It doesn't seem to matter if I'm interested or not. I still end up having to stop them and ask them to run it by me again.
Do you think you would zone out less often if you were listening to someone you find very interesting?

Someone very interesting? You know, I actually met someone fascinating just last week at the grocery store. A retired history professor. We were both looking at the apples—Honeycrisps, they were on sale for a dollar ninety-nine a pound, which is a steal these days. Used to be you could get a whole peck for that price when I was a kid. My mother would make these incredible apple pies every autumn. She had this special rolling pin, solid marble, weighed about ten pounds. My sister ended up taking it when mom passed, which caused a whole big fuss because I was the one who actually liked to bake...

But anyway, interesting people. Right. Well, like I keep trying to tell you, Doc, it really doesn't seem to make a difference who is doing the talking or how much I care about what they're saying. That's the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now. I'll be at the museum, and someone will be talking right to me about the art walk—which I love!—and I'm looking right at them. And then, boom. I realize I completely missed the middle part of whatever they just told me. I still just have to stop them and ask them to run it by me again. It's embarrassing, really.
Do you think your brain is processing the information but you're just not aware of it, or does it feel like you're completely missing the information when you zone out?

Processing the information... well, that sounds a bit like a computer, doesn't it? My grandson, Tommy, he just built one of those custom computers. Took over his mother's whole dining room table for three days. Wires and little metal chips everywhere. When he finally plugged it in and turned it on, the whole inside lit up neon blue. Looked just like a fish tank. I asked him why a computer needs to glow in the dark, and he started explaining something about cooling systems and processing power... I tell you, back in my day, if something had processing power, it was a food processor. My wife had this old Cuisinart, heavy as a bowling ball. Made the absolute best salsa in that thing. We used to grow our own tomatoes out back, big beefsteak ones... 

But anyway, sorry, you were asking about my brain processing things. 

You know, Doc, I feel terrible because I know I just keep giving you the exact same example over and over today, but it really is the only way I know how to describe it. It doesn't feel like the information is hiding in my head somewhere just waiting for me to process it. It feels like I completely miss it. Like it just never went in. That's really the whole reason I'm here—like I keep saying, I'll be at the museum, and they'll be talking right to me about the next art walk. I'm looking right at them, but then I realize I completely missed the middle of what they said. It's just a blank space. And I have to swallow my pride and ask them to run it by me again.
Do you feel like your mind is actively wandering to other thoughts when you zone out, or does it feel like you're just not taking in the information being presented to you?

Actively wandering? Well, sometimes I suppose I'm thinking about other things. Like the other day, I was wondering if I needed to get the gutters cleaned before the rainy season starts. You know, last year, the leaves from the big oak tree in the front yard completely clogged the downspout. Water was pouring right over the edge, flooding the flowerbeds. It washed away all the mulch I had just put down that spring. Cedar mulch, it was. Smelled wonderful when it was fresh, but it was a real pain to rake back into place once it dried out. I had to go buy two more bags just to fill in the bare spots. The guy at the garden center said I should put a screen over the gutters, but I don't know, those things always seem to cause more problems than they solve... 

But, oh, right, wandering thoughts. Well, to be honest, Doc—and I feel like a broken record here, I really do—it doesn't always feel like I'm thinking about gutters or anything else. Sometimes it just feels like the information never even arrives. Like I keep telling you, I'll be standing there at the museum, and someone is talking right to my face about the art walk. I'm looking right into their eyes, trying to pay attention, and then suddenly I just realize I have no idea what they said for the last minute or so. It's just gone. I didn't take it in at all, and I just have to stop them and say, "I'm sorry, can you run that by me again?"

patient.answer:
I definitely hear them talking. It's not my hearing, I had that checked a couple years ago. The guy at the clinic said my hearing was actually pretty good for a guy my age. doctor.intent: determine if the patient's mind wandering is triggered by stress or anxiety
doctor.question: Do you think you're more likely to zone out like that when you're feeling stressed or anxious about something?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms (zoning out/listening difficulty) are related to stress or anxiety, which is not covered by any specific symptom profile item in the provided list.

patient.answer:
Stress? No, I wouldn't really say it's stress. I mean, I don't have a whole lot to be stressed about these days, what with being retired and all. It's actually been real nice just taking it easy. My buddy Frank—he retired about five years before me—he always told me, "Just wait till you don't have to set an alarm clock anymore." And he was right, it's the best feeling in the world. Frank used to work down at the old auto plant before it closed up. Good guy, makes a mean brisket. He's got one of those big offset smokers in his backyard... takes him like fourteen hours to do a brisket right, but man, is it worth it. We usually go over there for the Fourth of July. 

But anyway, no, it's not really when I'm anxious. It just sort of happens whenever. I could be perfectly relaxed, just sitting there listening, and poof, my brain just takes a little vacation.

It's a nice little local history and art museum, nothing too fancy, but we get a good crowd on the weekends. We do these guided art walks through the galleries, and I used to love leading them. I'd read up on all the local artists... did you know we have a painter from around here who actually had a piece in the Smithsonian for a while? Eleanor something... Used to flood out the lower fields every spring. My uncle had a farm down that way, grew mostly corn and soybeans. He lost a whole crop one year to the flooding, just completely washed out. It was a real mess, took them weeks to clean up all the mud and debris that got left behind. 

But anyway, with the art walks... I just don't feel confident doing them anymore. I'll be right in the middle of explaining a piece, and I'll zone out, and then I lose my place and I'm just standing there looking at a group of people. And the other folks at the museum, Shirley and the rest of the board, I think they've noticed. They've been quietly shifting some of the planning pieces and the organizing stuff away from me. They're real nice about it, say they just want to "lighten my load," but I know it's because I keep missing things when we're having our meetings.

But, oh, right, wandering thoughts. Well, to be honest, Doc—and I feel like a broken record here, I really do—it doesn't always feel like I'm thinking about gutters or anything else. Sometimes it just feels like the information never even arrives. Like I keep telling you, I'll be standing there at the museum, and someone is talking right to my face about the art walk. I'm looking right into their eyes, trying to pay attention, and then suddenly I just realize I have no idea what they said for the last minute or so. It's just gone. I didn't take it in at all, and I just have to stop them and say, "I'm sorry, can you run that by me again?"

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of frequently zoning out and missing parts of conversations, despite being able to hear and see the person speaking, suggest a diagnosis of Other disorders of adult personality and behavior, specifically a condition characterized by difficulties with attention and processing information.
